title: Where the River Sleeps
author: Lantern Original
summaryTr: İstanbul'da bir kemancı çırağı, tamire getirilen eski ve çirkin bir kemanın içinde gizli bir harita bulur. Peşindeki zarif ama acımasız adamdan kaçarken onu Kapadokya'nın altındaki karanlık bir nehrin ve çanların gizemine götürür.
paragraphs: ## Chapter 1: The Violin Nobody Wanted
The man in the grey gloves offered five thousand euros for a broken violin, and Elif Arslan nearly dropped her cup of tea.

It was a wet Thursday afternoon in Kadıköy, Istanbul. Rain ran down the windows of Usta Nuri's workshop, and inside it was warm and smelled of wood and glue. Violins hung from the ceiling like strange fruit. Elif had worked here for three years, since she was twenty. She could repair a cracked back, change a bridge and match an old colour so well that even Usta Nuri could not find the repair.

The violin on the workbench was the ugliest in the shop. Its back was cracked, three strings were missing, and a long scratch ran across the top of the neck. Usta Nuri had bought it for eighty euros at a house sale in Vienna, because, as he said, he felt sorry for it.

"My name is Gregor Voss," said the man, and he gave a small bow. He was tall and thin, with a soft German accent, and he never took off his gloves. "I buy and sell old instruments. Five thousand euros. It is a generous offer, I think."
"It is a crazy offer," said Usta Nuri. He was seventy years old, and he was not afraid of anybody. "Why do you want it?"
"I like broken things." Voss smiled with his mouth, but not with his eyes. "Please, name your price."
"My price is six hundred euros, after my apprentice has repaired it. Come back in a week."
"Of course," said Voss. "I will come back." He put a white card on the bench and walked out into the rain.

Usta Nuri watched him go. "Nobody pays five thousand euros for that violin," he said. "Either that man is mad, or this violin is not what it seems." Then he took his umbrella and said that he was going to the tea house to meet his old friends, as he did every Thursday. "Don't work too late," he told Elif. Of course, she worked late.

By eight o'clock the street was quiet. Elif opened the cracked back of the violin with a thin flat knife, slowly, the way you open an old box. Dust fell out. Then she stopped. Something was glued to the inside of the top plate: a flat packet, wrapped in dark cloth and tied with thread.

Her hands were shaking when she cut the thread. Inside the cloth there were two things. The first was a small brass key, and the top of the key was shaped like a bell. The second was a sheet of thin paper, folded eight times.

She opened it on the bench, under the lamp. It was a map, drawn in black ink by a careful hand. A wavy line was a river. Above it there was a round sun with rays, and under the sun, seven little doors in a row. Next to the river was a drawing of a bell. At the bottom were two lines of German words that she could not read, and a date: October 1943. Above the date were three more words: Für Marta.
"Who are you, Marta?" Elif whispered.
Then the bell above the shop door rang.
"Usta? You're early!" She turned round. Gregor Voss was standing in the doorway with rain on his shoulders. He closed the door behind him, and she heard the key turn in the lock.
"Good evening, Miss Arslan," he said. "I'm afraid I was not honest this afternoon. I don't like broken things. I have been looking for that violin for eleven years."
He walked slowly towards the workbench. "Emil Hartmann, Vienna, 1943. Does the name mean anything to you?"
"No."
"Good. Then you know nothing, and that is lucky for you. Now give me what was inside the violin."
Elif held the map behind her back. The key was in her other hand, hidden in her fist. "I don't know what you mean," she said.
Voss smiled and took one more step. "I think you do."
## Chapter 2: The Last Ferry
Elif did not think. Her free hand found the cord of the workshop lamp and pulled, and the lamp crashed to the floor. The room went black.
"Dragan!" Voss shouted. "The back door!"

She jumped onto the workbench, pushed open the little window above the glue shelf and squeezed through it like a cat. She landed in a puddle in the alley, and cold rain hit her face. She pushed the map into her jacket and the key into her jeans pocket, and she ran.

Behind her a door opened, and heavy steps followed. She did not look back. She knew who it was: the big man in the black coat who had been standing in the courtyard. He was one of the biggest men she had ever seen.

The market in Kadıköy was almost closed, but the fish sellers were still washing their stalls. Elif ran between boxes of ice and fish. "Sorry! Excuse me! Sorry!" A man shouted at her. She ran through a baker's shop, in at the front door and out at the back, past a surprised cat and a very surprised baker. The steps behind her were slower now, but they were not far away.

Then she heard a crash and a loud shout in a language she did not know. She looked back for one second. Dragan was lying on the wet stones with an enormous fish on his chest, and an angry fish seller was hitting him with a wet cloth.
"Sorry!" Elif shouted again, and this time she really meant it.

She reached the pier just as the last ferry to Karaköy was leaving. The ropes were already off. Between the pier and the boat there was a gap of black water, one metre wide, then one and a half. Elif jumped. For a moment there was nothing under her feet. Then her hands and knees hit the deck. A sailor shouted at her, and an old man offered her his hand, laughing.

From the deck she could see them on the pier, small under the lights: the big man holding his side, and next to him, tall and still, Gregor Voss. He did not shout. He looked at her across the water, lifted one grey glove as if he was saying goodbye, and took out his phone.

Elif sat down among the tired people going home and shook. When her fingers worked again, she called Usta Nuri. She told him everything in one breath. "Stay where you are," he said. "I'll call the police." Ten minutes later he phoned back. The shop door was open and the lamp was broken, but nothing was missing. Voss had wanted only one thing.
"Send me a photograph of the map," said Usta Nuri.
She did. For a long time the line was silent.

"Elif," he said at last, "I learned German when I studied violin making in Germany, and I can read this. It says: Where the river sleeps, the bells sing. And here, next to the sun: Count seven doors from the sun."
"And Marta? Who is Marta?"

"I knew a Marta Hartmann once. She was my first violin teacher, when I was a small boy. She came to Istanbul from Vienna in 1943, when she was a child. She told us that her father had hidden something before he died, but she never found out where. She also lost her violin on the journey." He stopped. "She is ninety-four now. She lives in Moda. Elif, that ugly violin..."
"Where are the seven doors, Usta?"
"A river, a sun, doors in the rock." He thought. "I know only one place in Turkey with thousands of doors in the rock. Cappadocia."

Elif thought of Joaquín, a Chilean cave guide who lived in Göreme. They had met at a music festival two years before. She called him, and he answered happily at ten o'clock at night. She sent him the photograph. This time it was Joaquín who was silent. "Elif," he said, "I think I know this place. Come tomorrow."
"Go to the police," said Usta Nuri, when she told him her plan. "They will come to the shop, and I'll tell them everything."
"Voss knows I have the map, Usta. If I stay here, he will find me. If I go, I can find the place before he does."
"You are as stubborn as an old donkey," said Usta Nuri, and she could hear that he was proud. "Call me every hour."

At eleven o'clock, Elif was in the last row of the night bus to Nevşehir, with her jacket zipped up over the map. Voss is in Istanbul, she told herself. He can't know where I'm going. The bus began to move. Rain ran down the windows. Then, at the very last second, the doors opened again, and a big man in a black coat climbed in.

It was Dragan. He had a wet shirt, a red mark on his face and a smell of fish. He walked slowly down the aisle and sat down two rows in front of her. Then he turned his head and smiled. It was not a friendly smile.
Voss, it seemed, knew exactly where she was going. And in front of them lay seven hours of road.
## Chapter 3: Seven Doors from the Sun

Elif made a plan: stay awake, sit near the driver and don't look at Dragan. It was a bad plan, but she had no other. She moved to the front of the bus, and in the dark window she could see Dragan watching her, like a cat watching a bird.

At three in the morning the bus stopped at a large rest area in the middle of nowhere. There were bright lights, a café, big trucks, and tired passengers going in for tea. "Ten minutes," said the driver. Dragan stood up too. Elif went into the café, and he followed, a few steps behind her, like a shadow in a black coat.

At the biggest table, twelve women in colourful scarves were drinking tea and singing. A banner on their minibus said: Hacer Teyze's Pensioners' Club, Trip to Cappadocia. The oldest woman, small and round, with laughing eyes, saw Elif's frightened face. Then she saw Dragan.
"Teyze," said Elif quietly, "a man is following me. Please."
Hacer Teyze did not ask a single question. She looked at Dragan for a long time. "He looks like a wardrobe in a coat," she said. "Girls! We have a guest!"
In four seconds, Elif had a flowery scarf on her head, a cardigan on her shoulders and a glass of tea in her hand. She was sitting in the middle of twelve women who were all talking at once.
Dragan stopped at the table. "Excuse me," he said. "I am looking for a girl—"
"A girl?" Hacer Teyze stood up. She was shorter than his chest. "Which girl? Are you looking at our granddaughters? At this hour? Have you no shame?"
"No, I only—"

A handbag hit his arm. Another hit his back. "Go and sit down!" "Go back to your mother!" The women's voices got louder and louder, and the whole café watched a very large man run across the room, chased by twelve women with handbags.

From the café window, Elif watched Dragan stand on the steps of the bus. He looked left and right. The driver was waving, and he had a schedule to keep. In the end, Dragan got on. The doors closed, and the bus drove away without them.
"Now you travel with us, my child," said Hacer Teyze. "Eat something."

Elif slept with her head on Hacer Teyze's shoulder and a bag of dried apricots in her hand. When she woke up, the sky was pink, and it was full of hot-air balloons, hundreds of them, red and yellow and blue, rising slowly over a country of strange rock towers and caves. "Welcome to Cappadocia," said Hacer Teyze.
Joaquín was waiting outside his guesthouse in Göreme, a tall man with curly hair, a muddy jacket and two big backpacks. "You look terrible," he said.
"Thank you. It was a long night."
He looked at the map for a long time. "Where did you find this?"
"Inside a violin."

"Of course. Where else?" He laughed, then stopped. "Elif, it's the Sun House. In Pigeon Valley, forty minutes from here. It's a cliff with a round window, high in the rock. The tourists say it was a church. Under the window there are lots of doors, but most of them are old pigeon houses. A thousand years ago, the farmers made holes in the rock for the birds, because pigeon droppings are good for the fields."
"Pigeon droppings?"
"Life is not always romantic, Elif."

They walked into the valley in the early morning, between pink and white rocks, with ropes and helmets and lamps on their backs. On the way, Elif told him everything. Joaquín listened and said nothing, but now and then he looked at the sky. In the south, over the mountains, black clouds were piling up.

"Where the river sleeps," he said. "Many valleys here have dry riverbeds. They sleep for months. Then it rains in the mountains, forty kilometres away, and the river wakes up, without any warning." He shook his head. "It's all right. It's raining there, not here. If it was raining here, I would never take you underground."
"Not yet," said Elif.
The Sun House was a cliff, a hundred metres wide, with a perfect round window in the middle, like an eye. Under it there was a row of doors, big and small, black against the pink stone.
"Count seven doors from the sun," Elif read.
"Left or right?"
She looked at the map. "On the map they go to the right."

They counted aloud. One. Two. Three. The fourth door was huge. The fifth had a broken wall. The sixth was only a hole. The seventh was very small, at the foot of the rock, half hidden by a thorn bush. Joaquín pushed through the thorns and went in.
Inside there was a small room with hundreds of little holes in the walls. On the floor, in the dust, was a round hole, just wide enough for a man.
"Pigeon houses don't have holes in the floor," said Joaquín slowly. He shone his lamp down. It was very deep.

He tied the rope to a rock and went down first. Elif followed, her heart beating like a drum. The shaft was narrow, and the walls were cold. After six or seven metres, her lamp found old iron steps in the rock. She was thinking that someone had built them a very long time ago, for a reason. Then she heard stones falling above her, and a voice.
"Thank you, Miss Arslan."
She looked up. In the small circle of light there was a face, and a grey glove holding the rope.

"Dragan told me which bus you took," said Gregor Voss. "A plane is faster than a bus. And you have been so helpful, you and your friend. I don't like caves, so I will wait up here until you have opened the door. Then I will come down."
He let go of the rope. It fell past her into the dark.

"Please be careful," Voss said, almost kindly. The circle of light became a half circle. There was a scraping sound as a big flat stone slid across the hole. Then there was only a thin line of light, and then nothing.
The darkness was complete. For a moment, Elif could hear only her own breathing.
"Elif," said Joaquín's voice from below, very calm. "Don't panic."
"I'm not panicking."
"Good. Because I am."
## Chapter 4: The Bronze Door

Joaquín climbed back up the iron steps and pushed the stone with his back until his face was red. It did not move. "All right," he said at last. "So we go forward. Cave rule number one: never panic. Rule number two: if you panic, do it quietly."
Elif laughed a little. It helped.

At the bottom of the shaft, a low passage led into the rock. It was so narrow that they had to crawl on their elbows, with their lamps touching the stone. Elif hated small spaces, and she kept her eyes on Joaquín's boots. He talked to her all the time about nothing: his mother's cooking, a cow that fell into a cave once. Then she felt wind on her face. "Wind," said Joaquín happily. "Wind means there is somewhere for it to come from."
After fifty metres, the passage opened suddenly into a tall, wide tunnel. The lamps could not reach the roof. The floor was smooth like the inside of a bowl.
"This is a riverbed," said Joaquín, and he lifted his lamp. High above their heads, a dark line ran along the wall. "That's the water mark. When the river is awake, it fills the tunnel up to there."
"But it's dry now."
"Now. The river is sleeping."
Elif looked at the map in her hand and felt cold.

They walked along the riverbed for ten minutes. Then she heard a tiny sound. Ting. She stopped. Ahead of them, hanging from the roof on thin chains, was a line of small bronze bells, fifty or a hundred of them, right across the tunnel. They shone like gold in the lamplight. One was still swinging; Joaquín's helmet had touched it. Ting, it sang again, and the sound ran away down the tunnel.
"Where the river sleeps, the bells sing," whispered Elif. "They're not decoration. They're an alarm. When the water comes, it pushes the air in front of it, and the air moves the bells."
"Who builds an alarm for a river?"
"Someone who hid something very important here, and wanted people to leave in time."
They walked under the bells very slowly, with their arms close to their bodies, and neither of them breathed.

Behind the bells, in the rock wall, there was a round bronze door, green with age. In the middle was a keyhole in the shape of a little bell. Elif's hand was shaking. The brass key slid in, turned, and clicked. They pushed together. With a sound like a long sigh, the door opened.

The room beyond was round, dry and cold, and it smelled of old wood. Joaquín's lamp moved slowly over the walls, and for a while neither of them spoke. Shelves cut into the rock held cases: black, brown and green, small and long, dozens and dozens of them. Each had a paper label in a neat hand. Prague Quartet, 1938. Mr. A. Weiss, cello. Miss Rosa Klein, viola.

Elif opened the nearest case with trembling fingers. A violin lay on dark red velvet. The wood shone like honey, as perfect as on the day it was made. She knew from the colour of the varnish what it was. "This one violin," she whispered, "is worth more than Usta Nuri's whole street."

On a stone table in the middle of the room lay a leather notebook and a folded letter. The letter was in German, but under every line someone had written the English words too, as if Emil Hartmann wanted anybody to be able to read it. Joaquín read it aloud, in his careful voice.

"My dear Marta. If you are reading this, you are grown up and the war is over. These instruments belong to musicians who had to run away from their homes. I could not save the people, but I could save their music. Please find their families and give them back. Do not be afraid of the river. Listen to the bells. Your loving father, Emil."

The notebook was a list of names and addresses. Elif turned the pages slowly. There were forty names. Forty families had been waiting for eighty years. Joaquín folded the letter and slid it back inside the notebook.
Then, behind them, there was a tiny sound. Ting.
They turned. Far away down the tunnel, one bell was moving by itself. Joaquín's face changed. "That isn't us," he said.
A second bell began to move. Then four. And from the other end of the tunnel, where the shaft was, two lights came towards them, and a calm voice said: "Thank you both. That is far enough."
Gregor Voss walked out of the dark with Dragan behind him. He was smiling. And above their heads, one by one, all the bells began to sing.
## Chapter 5: The River Wakes
Voss stepped into the bronze room and looked around like a man in a dream. "Eleven years," he whispered. "Dragan, the cases. All of them."
"Mr. Voss," said Joaquín, "listen to the bells."
"Pretty, aren't they?"
"It rained in the mountains this morning. The river is waking up. We have a few minutes, no more."
"A lovely story," said Voss.
But Dragan was not moving. He was looking at the bells. "Boss," he said. "They are ringing very loudly."
"It is the wind."
Then they all heard it: far away, a low sound, like a train in a tunnel. It grew louder every second. Dragan's face went grey. Voss's smile died.

Elif's eyes ran round the room. Emil Hartmann had built an alarm for the river. He would not have built it without a way out. Behind the last shelf, in the shadow, she saw iron steps in the rock, going up into a narrow black hole.
"There!" she shouted. She grabbed the leather notebook from the table, pushed it inside her jacket, and snatched up the case with the honey-coloured violin. "That's the way out! Joaquín, go!"

"Take them!" Voss screamed at Dragan. "Take as many as you can!" He picked up two cases himself, and Dragan took three. But the iron steps were narrow, and nobody can climb a ladder with two cases in their arms.

The sound became a wall. The water hit the bronze door like a hand and threw it back against the rock. Brown, foaming water poured into the room, knee deep in a few seconds. The shelves fell, and cases floated like boats.

Elif climbed with the case under one arm. The steps were wet and cold, and the water was rising behind her like an animal. Joaquín was just below her, pushing her feet up. Thirty steps, forty. At the top, a round wooden cover blocked the way. Joaquín pushed with his shoulder. Nothing.
"Again!"
They pushed together, and with a groan the cover moved. Light! Rain! Grass! Elif crawled out onto the wet ground inside the walls of a ruined stone chapel, and Joaquín fell out after her.

Below them, Dragan was climbing hard. He had dropped the cases. Voss was behind him, still holding his two, with the water around his chest. "Wait!" he shouted. "Wait for me!" Dragan reached the top, and his foot slipped. Joaquín caught his collar, Elif caught Joaquín's belt, and together they pulled. Dragan landed on the grass like a big wet fish.
"The cases!" Voss screamed from the hole. "Somebody take the cases!"
Elif looked at Joaquín. Joaquín looked at the water. "Drop them!" Elif shouted. "Give me your hand!"

For a second, Voss did not move. Then he opened his arms. The two cases fell into the brown water and floated away into the dark, and he reached up with his bare hand. They pulled him out too. He lay on the grass in the rain, his expensive coat brown with mud, and his grey gloves were gone.
"Good morning, Mr. Voss," said a voice.

Six police officers stood in the rain around the ruined chapel. Beside them was Usta Nuri with an umbrella, and next to him, in a wheelchair under a blanket, sat a very small old woman with white hair. Nuri had taken the first plane from Istanbul that morning, and he had not come alone. The old lady had said that she had waited eighty years and could not wait another day.

She looked at the muddy man on the ground. "Voss," she said quietly. Her voice was weak, but nobody in the chapel moved. "Your grandfather bought my father's shop in Vienna in 1941, for the price of a loaf of bread. He wanted my father's instruments, too. I see that the Voss family never gives up." Two officers lifted Voss to his feet. He did not say a word.

Elif walked across the wet grass. She was still holding the case in one hand. With the other she took the leather notebook out of her jacket and put it into the old woman's thin hands. "Your father left this for you, Mrs. Hartmann," she said. "There is a letter inside."
Marta Hartmann looked at the first page. Her fingers were shaking. "Vati," she whispered, and she began to cry.

Later, Joaquín said the river had gone down by the evening, as fast as it had come. The bronze room was high in the rock, and the heavy door had closed itself again. Most of the cases on the upper shelves were dry. In the next two years, thirty-one instruments went home to families in nine countries. The first one, the honey-coloured violin that Elif had carried out of the cave, went back to a family in Prague.

A week after the flood, Elif sat in the workshop in Kadıköy, closing the back of the old violin. She had found the crack, cleaned the glue, and matched the colour of the wood so well that nobody could find the repair. Usta Nuri put on the new strings himself. On Friday, a car stopped outside, and Marta Hartmann came in with a blanket on her knees.

Elif put the violin into her hands. Marta looked for a long time at the scratch on the top of the neck. "An M," she said. "I made it with a pin when I was nine. My father was so angry." Slowly, she lifted the violin to her chin. Her bow was shaking. For a moment nothing happened, and then she played three notes, a slow, soft song from a city that she had left eighty years before.
Elif's phone buzzed in her pocket. It was a message from Joaquín, with a photograph of the tunnel. The water was gone, and the bells were hanging quietly from the roof.
The river is sleeping again, he had written.

glossary.bridge: (kemanda) eşik, tellerin üzerinde durduğu küçük parça
glossary.shaft: dikey kuyu, dar ve derin boşluk

quiz.q: Why does Gregor Voss visit the workshop at the start of the story?
options: He wants to learn to repair violins
He wants to buy a broken violin for a lot of money
He wants to sell a map to Usta Nuri
He wants to meet Marta Hartmann
quiz.explainTr: Voss, bozuk kemana beş bin euro teklif eder; çünkü içinde gizli bir şey olduğunu bilir.

quiz.q: What does Elif find inside the violin?
quiz.explainTr: Elif kemanın içinde zil biçimli bir pirinç anahtar ve ince kâğıda çizilmiş bir harita bulur.

quiz.q: How does Elif escape from Dragan at the rest area?
options: A group of older women protects her
quiz.explainTr: Hacer Teyze ve arkadaşları Elif'i saklar ve el çantalarıyla Dragan'ı kovalar.

quiz.q: What do the bronze bells in the tunnel do?
options: They show where the instruments are
They warn that the river is coming
quiz.explainTr: Çanlar bir alarm görevi görür: nehir uyandığında su havayı iter ve çanları çalar.

quiz.q: What is hidden in the round room behind the bronze door?
options: Musical instruments that belonged to musicians who had to leave their homes
quiz.explainTr: Oda, evlerinden kaçmak zorunda kalan müzisyenlerin kemanlarla dolu; Emil Hartmann bunları saklamıştı.
